processing: Shoots of one bud with one or two leaves are fixed, rolled, rubbed to raise down, shaped into small curls and dried.
harvest_season: Traditionally begins a few days after Qingming on the island, though pre-Qingming lots are also sold today.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, spiral curls of glossy green with visible down, sometimes likened to small hooks or tadpoles.
appearance_wet: Buds and leaves opening into small clusters.
taste_profile: Fresh and brisk with a clean sweetness, and an orchid note is often mentioned.

brewing.notes: Down clouds the first cup, which is normal. Curled, downy greens like this one do well with water poured onto the leaf gently in a glass.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring tea, with pre-Qingming lots at the top of the range, and best within the year.
description:
Putuo Fo Cha, 'Putuo Buddha tea', is the green of Mount Putuo and the surrounding Zhoushan islands, off the coast of Zhejiang. Few well-known Chinese greens grow on islands, and its sea fog and monastery setting are the heart of its identity.

The tea grows on sun-facing slopes and in sheltered hollows, with plenty of cloud around the summit. Shoots are fixed, rolled, and rubbed into tight curls that show their down, so it looks closer to a Bi Luo Chun than a Long Jing.

The cup is bright yellow-green, fresh and brisk, with a clean sweetness and sometimes orchid. Cooler water keeps those notes; the small curls release quickly, so short steeps work well.

The name is a protected trademark, and the tea is grown on Putuo and elsewhere in Zhoushan. Ask where it was grown and the harvest date.
history:
Tea on Putuo is tied to its Buddhist monasteries, where monks are said to have grown it for offerings; accounts place the beginnings around the Tang, which is hard to verify. Small amounts were offered to pilgrims in the early Qing, and growth followed when ferries brought more visitors in the late Qing. Older tea here is said to have been sun-dried, unlike today's.

It was listed as tribute in the Guangxu reign and took a second prize at the 1915 Panama exposition. It became a registered geographical indication trademark in 2008, and by 2017 plantings across Zhoushan reached 270 hectares.
